clue.text: General drudge for the Kennel Club?

definitions.meaning: a menial worker who does all the tedious jobs nobody else wants
the Kennel Club is the British organisation governing pedigree canines, so whimsically a body made up of hounds

explanation.surface: Someone wonders who does the menial chores at the society for pedigree pets.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the answer as DOG'S BODY: the Kennel Club is the UK's governing organisation for pedigree breeds.
explanation.definitionFit: A general drudge is a lowly servant doing every chore, the classic meaning of this informal British term.

clue.text: Stop religious believer imprisoning saint

indicators.note: the believer's word holds the saint's letter inside it, like a cell

parts.note: a deist believes in a creator God but not in revelation

explanation.surface: A devout person is told to halt after locking up a holy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'imprisoning' puts S inside DEIST, after DE.
explanation.definitionFit: To desist is to cease or leave off an action, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Boxer Corbett said to train here shortly

definitions.text: Boxer Corbett said to train here shortly

parts.words: Boxer Corbett said to train here shortly
parts.note: the boxer 'Gentleman Jim' Corbett's first name, spoken, sounds like the abbreviated name of a place for exercise

explanation.surface: A remark that the champion boxer Corbett would soon be training at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: James J. Corbett, 'Gentleman Jim', was a world heavyweight champion of the 1890s. JIM said out loud is GYM, the short form of the full word.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnasium is a hall equipped for physical training and exercise, often shortened to its first three letters.

clue.text: Amelia's mistake in fashion?

parts.note: Amelia ... promoted loose trousers for women, so a fashion lapse of hers shares her surname, which also means a howler

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Amelia committed a sartorial blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: Amelia Bloomer was a nineteenth-century American campaigner for women's dress reform whose name was given to baggy trousers; a 'bloomer' is also British slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is an informal word for a blunder or howler; Amelia Bloomer's dress reform gave her name to an item of fashion.

clue.text: Games so indecisive, as lots are

definitions.meaning: matches that end level with no winner
lots are pulled out of a hat or bag when deciding by chance

explanation.surface: Matches end without a result, just as raffle tickets are pulled out.
explanation.definitionFit: A tied game is described as drawn; lots are drawn when chosen by chance.

clue.text: Climbed like a fish

definitions.meaning: went up, as a mountaineer goes up a rock face
having a skin covered in small protective plates, as most fish do

explanation.definitionFit: Climbed is a synonym for ascended a wall; a fish's skin has small horny plates, so it is covered in them.

clue.text: Fancy putting him in care anyway

indicators.note: the pronoun is placed inside the rearranged letters
anyway, read as 'any way', means in any order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone suggests putting a man into care regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' rearranges CARE to CERA, and 'in' puts HIM inside it after C.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimera is a wild fantasy or illusion, matching fancy used as a noun for an imagined notion.

clue.text: Language not quite dead in ceremonial use

definitions.text: Language not quite dead in ceremonial use

parts.words: Language not quite dead in ceremonial use
parts.note: a classical tongue no longer spoken day to day but still heard in church rites and university ceremonies

explanation.surface: A description of an old tongue that survives in rituals.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin is called a dead language but survives in the Catholic Mass and degree ceremonies, so it is 'not quite dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin, the ancient Roman tongue, is no longer a native speech yet persists in liturgy and formal Oxford and Cambridge rituals.

clue.text: Prudent to be separate, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard as spoken rather than as written

parts.note: discrete means separate or distinct

explanation.surface: It is wise to keep apart, someone suggests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks a homophone: DISCRETE (separate) is pronounced exactly like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being discreet means being careful and tactful in what one says or does, which is a sense of prudent.

clue.text: Time thereby taken by rosebud gatherers?

definitions.text: Time thereby taken by rosebud gatherers?

parts.words: Time thereby taken by rosebud gatherers?
parts.note: 'take time by the' tuft of hair on the brow means seize the moment, as Herrick urged with 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may'

explanation.surface: A question about how those picking roses grab the moment.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's poem 'To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time' begins 'Gather ye rosebuds while ye may'; the idiom 'take time by the forelock' means seize an opportunity.
explanation.definitionFit: A forelock is the lock of hair above the brow; Father Time is pictured with one, to be grasped when opportunity comes.

clue.text: Milton's tragedy finally brought the house down

definitions.meaning: John Milton's verse drama of 1671 about the blinded Hebrew strongman
at the end of the story the strongman pulls down the pillars of the Philistine temple, killing all inside

explanation.definitionFit: Milton's closet drama tells of the Biblical hero whose last act was toppling the temple; 'brought the house down' also means drew huge applause.

clue.text: Chap after Matilda a tramp — or a burglar?

definitions.meaning: in the Australian song Waltzing Matilda, 'Matilda' is the bedroll carried by the wandering hero
an Australian itinerant worker carrying his belongings in a bundle
whimsically, a man with swag, the loot a thief carries off

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the fellow pursuing a girl called Matilda is a vagrant or a housebreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: Waltzing Matilda is Australia's unofficial anthem; 'Matilda' there is a bedroll, not a girl, and the singer who carries it is a wandering bush worker.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australia the term means an itinerant labourer humping his bundle; 'swag' is also a thief's haul, hence the joking burglar.

clue.text: Eastern king receives no lady from Aquitaine

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for east or eastern

indicators.note: the king's name takes in the other word, which sits inside it

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.surface: An oriental monarch is turned down by a noblewoman from south-west France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'receives' puts NO inside LEAR. Eleanor of Aquitaine was the twelfth-century duchess who married two kings, of France and of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Aquitaine was the famous medieval duchess and queen who ruled that region of France.

clue.text: Unusual toil in which Harte produced book of opera

indicators.note: the writer's first name is placed inside the rearranged letters
something unusual is out of the ordinary, so these letters appear in a different order

parts.note: Bret Harte was the American writer of Wild West stories; his first name is wanted

explanation.surface: A writer labours unusually hard to produce the words for an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unusual' rearranges TOIL to LITO, and 'in which' puts BRET inside it after LI. Bret Harte was a nineteenth-century American author of frontier tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A libretto is the text, or book, of an opera or musical, written by a librettist for the composer.

clue.text: First to rise — not second — fish is fooling

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the letters read upwards, from bottom to top
not tells us to leave out the letter that follows

parts.note: ling is a long-bodied fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A fish is the first to rise, never the second, and is just messing about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes S (second) from FIRST to give FIRT, and 'to rise' turns it upward into TRIF before LING.
explanation.definitionFit: Trifling and fooling both mean idly toying or messing about rather than acting seriously.

clue.text: Early settler here, right in the corner of the square

definitions.meaning: one of the Germanic peoples who settled in Britain in the fifth century

definitions.text: right in the corner of the square
definitions.meaning: each corner of a square makes a ninety-degree figure, known as a right one

explanation.surface: A pioneer here takes up a spot at the corner of the village green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'here' points at England, named after these settlers; 'right' belongs to the second reading, a right angle.
explanation.definitionFit: The Angles were among the first Germanic settlers of England; the corner of a square forms a right-angled meeting of two lines.

clue.text: Gentleman's first in position outside a flash pub

indicators.note: first means take only the opening letter of the word gentleman
the word for position goes around the single letter

parts.note: a place is a position or location

explanation.surface: A gentleman is the first inside a smart bar in a good location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' puts PLACE around A, giving PALACE after G and IN. A gin palace was a gaudily decorated Victorian pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A gin palace was a showy, brightly lit Victorian public house, the kind of flashy bar where spirits flowed.

clue.text: This sea has fuel, thus supporting rising artists

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting pieces sit underneath, coming after
in a down clue rising means read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, so RAS are artists
gas is a fuel
so means thus or therefore

explanation.surface: A sea holds fuel, so it keeps artists afloat as they come up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns RAS to SAR, and 'supporting' puts GAS + SO beneath it in the down grid. The Sargasso Sea is in the North Atlantic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sargasso Sea is a region of the North Atlantic noted for floating seaweed, an example of a sea.

clue.text: Allow many into opening of mine

indicators.note: the letter for a large number is placed inside the word for a mine entrance

parts.note: an adit is a horizontal entrance tunnel to a mine
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so a great many

explanation.surface: Many people are let into the entrance of a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening of mine' looks like a first-letter instruction, but it defines ADIT, a mine's horizontal entrance shaft.
explanation.definitionFit: To admit is to allow in, or to permit someone entry, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Spear I had thrust in the river

indicators.note: the contracted pronoun phrase is pushed inside the river's name

parts.note: the Trent is a major river of the English Midlands
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: Someone recalls pushing a spear into the water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrust in' puts ID inside TRENT, England's third-longest river, after TR.
explanation.definitionFit: A trident is a three-pronged spear, carried by Neptune and used for fishing.

clue.text: Writer's sources here of various kinds, including colour

indicators.note: the rearranged letters take the colour word inside them
various suggests different forms, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: tan is a yellowish-brown colour

explanation.surface: Someone describes where a writer's materials of many sorts, including coloured ones, are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various' rearranges KINDS to INKSD, and 'including' puts TAN inside it after INKS.
explanation.definitionFit: An inkstand is a desk stand holding pots of ink, the source a pen-and-ink writer draws on.

clue.text: Figurine of jade discovered in old Irish hill

indicators.note: something discovered in a place is found inside it, so the horse word sits within the hill

parts.note: Tara is the hill in County Meath, seat of the ancient High Kings of Ireland
a jade is a worn-out horse, as is a nag

explanation.surface: A small statue carved of green stone turns up in an ancient Irish mound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jade' looks like the green stone, but here means a tired old horse, NAG. Tanagra figurines are small Greek terracottas named after a town in Boeotia.
explanation.definitionFit: Tanagra figures are small painted terracotta statuettes from ancient Greece, named after the town where they were found.

clue.text: A term for a man of property? On the contrary

definitions.text: A term for a man of property? On the contrary

parts.words: A term for a man of property? On the contrary
parts.note: flip the phrase: not a word describing a property owner, but a person who holds property for a fixed period

explanation.surface: A question about what a property owner is called, then a reversal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'on the contrary', the clue becomes 'a man of property for a term': someone who holds a property for a fixed lease period.
explanation.definitionFit: A lessee is the tenant who holds land or a building under a lease for a fixed span, not the owner who grants it.

clue.text: Hardy Oak bore a divine message

definitions.meaning: The shepherd hero of Thomas Hardy's novel Far from the Madding Crowd
the archangel who carried God's announcement to Mary

explanation.surface: A sturdy oak tree carried a message from heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' looks like an adjective for a tough tree; it is the novelist Thomas Hardy, whose shepherd hero shares a name with the archangel of the Annunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Hardy named his shepherd Gabriel Oak; the archangel of that name brought news of Christ's birth to Mary.

clue.text: Trimming assistance in support of certain transport

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits below, so it comes after

parts.note: BR is British Rail, the former UK national railway
aid means help or assistance

explanation.surface: Help comes to prop up a particular transport service, with cuts in mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trimming' looks like cutting back, but means decorative edging. BR was British Rail, the UK's state railway until the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: Braid is a woven decorative edging sewn onto uniforms and garments as ornamental trim.

clue.text: Its house occupied by Israelites in Egypt

definitions.text: Its house occupied by Israelites in Egypt

parts.words: Its house occupied by Israelites in Egypt
parts.note: the Bible calls Egypt 'the house of' this state, recalling the Hebrews' enslavement before the Exodus

explanation.surface: A clue about where the Hebrews lived during their time in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: Exodus 20:2 speaks of God bringing Israel 'out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage'; the house is a state, not a building.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israelites were enslaved in Egypt, and slavery or servitude is what the Biblical phrase names.

clue.text: Tea he found consumed by a snake

indicators.note: the pronoun is swallowed by the snake, sitting inside its name

parts.note: a boa is a large constricting snake

explanation.surface: A man finds himself eaten by a serpent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consumed by' puts HE inside BOA, after BO. Bohea is an old name for a black China tea.
explanation.definitionFit: Bohea was an eighteenth-century name for a black China tea from the Wuyi hills.

clue.text: Treacherous type of rat has seen kings ruined

indicators.note: ruined suggests wrecked, so these words are broken up and rebuilt in another order

explanation.surface: A disloyal rodent has watched monarchs brought low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges RATHASSEENKINGS. 'rat' tempts as the definition of a traitor, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden, deceitful enemy is likened to a serpent lurking unseen in the lawn, an old idiom for a false friend.

clue.text: Funny thing about the tree in Knox's deserted quad?

definitions.text: about the tree in Knox's deserted quad?
definitions.meaning: Ronald Knox's limerick says God must find it exceedingly odd that the tree continues to be when no one is about in the quad

explanation.surface: A curious puzzle about a tree standing in an empty college courtyard.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronald Knox's limerick on Berkeley's idealism asks whether a tree in an Oxford quadrangle still exists when nobody is there to see it; God thinks it 'exceedingly odd'.
explanation.definitionFit: A funny thing is a peculiarity or curiosity; the limerick's tree existing unobserved is called exceedingly strange.

clue.text: These swine a danger out east

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of their order and rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that pigs pose a threat out in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges A DANGER to GADAREN, then E for east follows. In the Gospels Jesus sent demons into the Gadarene herd, which ran into the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gadarene swine of the New Testament stampeded over a cliff after receiving the evil spirits Jesus cast out.
